content: 1. Sanitary inspection (SI) forms are specifically designed to evaluate ten dimensions of water supply systems, including construction and design, maintenance of the scheme, pollution risks, and the level of service provided. These inspections are particularly valuable in rural areas where water supply systems may be less developed. 2. The SI process is conducted using an iPad, which facilitates the collection of standardized data, provides easy access to information across various indicators, and enables the identification of high-risk facilities through automatically generated scores. 3. As water suppliers implement improvements, the risk assessments are updated as part of follow-up activities. This iterative process ensures that the risk management approach remains dynamic and responsive to changes. 4. The use of this digital tool has significantly enhanced the professionalism of health inspectors, as it enforces the use of standardized questions and specific formats for data collection. This has led to noticeable improvements in data quality and reduced variability in the information collected. 5. In Zambia, the National Water Supply and Sanitation Council (NWASCO), established in 2000, performs a wide range of regulatory functions. These include developing drinking-water standards and guidelines, formulating service-level agreements with water suppliers, monitoring water quality, reporting on performance, and applying incentives or sanctions as needed. 6. NWASCO reviews water quality data provided by Zambia’s 11 commercial utilities and conducts inspections and water quality testing to validate the data. A sustainable financing mechanism, primarily funded by a 2% levy on commercial utilities’ revenues and licensing fees, covers approximately 90% of NWASCO’s operational costs. 7. In Serbia, a nationwide survey in 2016 assessed sanitary inspection scores and Escherichia coli (E. coli) test results from over 1,300 rural water supplies. This joint assessment categorized E. coli counts and SI scores to determine relative risk levels and prioritize improvement actions. 8. Findings from Serbia revealed that approximately one-third of water samples did not meet microbial standards. Additionally, 30% of piped supplies and 40% of individual supplies were identified as having high or urgent priorities for improvement. 9. In Indonesia, environmental health workers conduct sanitary inspections (SIs) as part of a surveillance program mandated by a 2023 national decree. SI forms are tailored to the main types of water supply technologies, such as dug wells, spring water, rainwater harvesting, and piped networks. 10. During inspections in Indonesia, critical findings are discussed with service providers and water users on-site to ensure problems are understood and practical solutions are identified. Findings are subsequently entered into an electronic information management system for detailed reporting and follow-up. 11. In the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, the Ministry of Health oversees a surveillance program to ensure water safety. This involves testing for parameters such as chlorine, E. coli, nitrates, and heavy metals. Collaborative efforts between service providers, the water authority, and the Ministry address identified issues through additional testing, sanitary inspections, and water safety plan audits. 12. In Sierra Leone, efforts to improve rural water supply data management have included government-led national inventories and routine monitoring. However, challenges such as unclear institutional frameworks and limited technical capacity have hindered effective data use. 13. To address these challenges, Sierra Leone launched a National Digital Monitoring Approach in 2019, requiring all data to be shared on the global Water Point Data Exchange platform. This initiative aims to ensure routine monitoring informs district water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) plans. 14. In Mali, the government has developed WASH accounts to track sector financing and monitor progress toward national targets. Findings from the first WASH accounts cycle in 2016 revealed significant funding gaps, with average annual expenditures covering only 53% of identified needs. 15. Subsequent WASH accounts cycles in Mali expanded data collection to include water resource management, hygiene, and WASH in schools and health centers. These findings have informed funding dialogues, resulting in increased government and donor contributions to the sector. 16. Despite progress, Mali’s WASH sector funding remains insufficient to meet national targets. However, the development of WASH accounts has provided robust evidence to track progress and support decision-making for improved water and sanitation services.
